text: [Music] Toastmasters and guests, it is my
pleasure to welcome International President-Elect  Distinguished Toastmaster Margaret Page.
-Welcome to the 2021 World Championship of Public  Speaking Showcase. My name is Margaret Page,
and I am Toastmasters International  President-Elect and will be your emcee for this
showcase. Congratulations to all three contestants  who share this global virtual stage of the World
Championship of Public Speaking. Members and  guests, meet the 2021 World Championship winners:
World Champion Verity Price, second place winner  Nitay-Yair Levi, and our third-place winner
Roger Caesar. During today's showcase we are  going to speak with each winner for a few minutes.
But first I invite our new World Champion Verity  to enjoy two minutes to share acknowledgements
with our audience. Over to you, Verity. -Thank you so much, Margaret. I-I must
say two minutes to say what I have to say would  take a lifetime, but I have 120 seconds so I will
start with the two most important words which are  thank you. I’m so humbled and happy and grateful
to have received this title today, I’m going  to be pinching myself for weeks to come.
Thank you to my club Toasted Toastmasters,  to my incredible District 74 Southern Africa,
who have supported me and sent me messages saying  it's time for Africa—and today we discovered that
it was. I am blown away to be the first winner  of this title in Africa, I hope that I have
broken the proverbial four-minute mile for  all speakers on this incredible continent,
because I really believe that this title can  come back to Africa many, many times. Thank
you to my husband who has looked after our  little boy so I could stay in the bedroom and
deliver speeches at all the incredible clubs that  have opened their doors to me across the world;
it's been the most extraordinary journey. I want  to also give a big shout out to Pres Vasilev for
his amazing compelling storytelling course that  I bought at the start of my journey and used
to help me craft my final speech. And then my  really big shout out to my coach, Lance Miller.
My favorite World Champ of all time, and to have  had the privilege of have you coach me, Lance,
and bring me to this point, I’m absolutely blown  away. It's been extraordinary. But mostly to you,
to Toastmasters International, to the audiences  that have made this possible for all of us, and
to my fellow contestants to share this stage with  you, I know only three of us could be at the top,
but all eight speeches today blew me away. To my  semi-finalists, to all the dreams that were born
in this contest and they're gonna come back to the  stage next year, I can't wait to-to see what you
bring. But if I can leave you with nothing else,  it's that right now I’m sitting in a room similar
to one that for many years felt like a prison.  And today it's shown me that a prison can turn
into a platform. And coming from South Africa  where our biggest inspiration, Nelson Mandela,
took imprisonment and turned it into a platform  for change, I believe that as speakers and as
leaders we can all do that. So, thank you from  the bottom of my heart, I am so grateful to
be your world champion and I’m going to be  punching myself for days to come. Thank you.
-Thank you, Verity, for your gracious  and inspiring words. You have thanked a
lot of people along your personal journey who  have influenced your success up to this very
moment. These acknowledgments are indicators of  a true Toastmaster leader, congratulations again.
Later in the showcase we will ask the winners  questions submitted by those of you watching us
live today. If you would like to submit a  question, please use the Q&A feature on the
platform, type in your question and hit send.  We will do our very best to get to as many
questions as possible. But please be aware, we  may not have time to get to all your questions.
So first, I have a few questions for our winners.  I’d like to go back to Verity again and ask,
what does it feel like to  be the 2021 World Champion
of Public Speaking? Take us through the  range of emotions you have experienced in
the last few hours since you were declared  the World Champion of Public Speaking.
-Margaret, I think I will feel what it feels  like—tomorrow when I wake up—at the moment,
I honestly can say I feel like I’m in a bubble,  but I was so privileged I got to watch with a
whole lot of family and friends the first time in  a long time that I had quite a few people with me.
And when it was announced the joy around me  of the people that believe in me and support
me…I just felt like it flooded through my whole  body, and we danced, and we sang, and we just
celebrated. We felt like we'd won a world cup.  And I just feel so grateful, and I think-I think
for me right now what's-what's settling in is that  the last six months and everything I’ve learned,
now it's time for me to figure out how  I share that and how I give that back,
especially into my District and into my fellow  members. Because I’ve got lots that I can share
now to make this journey easier for the ones  who come behind me. But I’m just over the moon.
-And we can see that and feel that for  you. But many people would like to be in
your shoes right now and share what that  immediate onrush of attention feels like.
-Also overwhelming, I haven't had a chance to get  to all the messages. And they've been flooding in
throughout this journey from—and I’m sure all my  fellow contestants have had this since winning
Districts. You just have people that believe in  you, that reach out that take the time to send
messages on social media platforms or WhatsApp,  and I have felt so connected and I think the big
thing for me that's come through this journey  is, alone I can't, together we can. And I’m sure
all my contestants will agree, none of us have  given a speech that we wrote by ourselves.
It's from the feedback that we've received, that  we've implemented, we've changed, we've grown, so
I can't wait to get to all the messages and  reply to everyone, but wow. Thank you. Thank
you for everything that's flooding in. -Indeed. Together we can, right? Yeah.
So, Nitay-Yair, I’d like to go to you. How does  it feel to be the second-place winner of the ‘21
World Championship of Public Speaking? Um, take  us through the range of emotions you have felt.
-I-I don't-I don't still-I don't think I even  realized that here, you know, the-the magnitude
of that achievement. Uh, as Verity said, there's  a lot of work that goes straight, there's a lot
of people that help you, and-and just a moment in  time of something that had been happening for a
very long time and there's a lot of people  I need to thank, uh, for that moment. So,
I’ll echo Verity: I think only  tomorrow that will settle in
and only tomorrow I’ll realize what has been  achieved, and time to get ready for next year.
-Thank you, yes, indeed, tomorrow. Nitay-Yair,  what lasting impression do you hope your speech
made on the audience? If members  are talking about your speech
one year from now, what one thing  would you like them to be saying?
-In terms of the final speech is my message,  which perhaps sounds simple, but very hard to
do is to show love to those who are important to  you. Because they're there the whole time and you
take them sometime for granted. I have throughout  my past, especially with my mother which I love
very much. And it's very easy to-to take people  for granted. But they really shouldn't be,
because they love to use what propels you forward.  So, always show your love. Simple as that.
And as hard as it says-as it may not be to do. -Thank you for those beautiful words.
Roger, how does it feel to be there on this big  virtual platform as the third-place winner of
the ‘21 World Championship of Public Speaking? -It feels amazing. Absolutely amazing. It's
surreal, and I-I echo what  my fellow contestants said.
You-you go through all this process, the amount of  work, the-the coaching, the feedback that you get,
the support from all those around you, I  mean…you go through the entire process and
all you hope for is a chance. And that's what  it comes down to—a chance to get here so that
you could spread your message and be able to  inspire others. I mean for me in my message was
that—to inspire others to find their greatness  and I think by looking at all of these people,
Verity and Nitay-Yair and the other competitors  today…that's what they were doing: trying to
inspire our audience in our own way through our  stories, and make sure that they also can find
their greatness in some way, shape or form. So, I  am I’m thrilled, absolutely thrilled to be here.
-Well, we-we certainly found your  greatness. Roger, what inspired you
to write and speak about what has now become  your winning speech, entitled, “Is it in you?”
-Well, I’ll take you back to the speech that I  did in the semi-finals and…my father and I have
had this relationship where there are moments when  I was just cringing about him, and then there are
moments when I realized, “Wow he's such a great  man.” And my mom has always been that verbal
influence in my life, and I felt  that it was important that I
bring the two together and show how  much they have meant to me. My parents
mean the world to me. My sister, yeah, she  means something to me too…she will not be
singing anywhere, and that is okay with me,  but she means a lot to me. But my parents,
they have done so much hard work throughout the  years and the lessons that I have learned along
the way have been so instrumental in who I am  today and I’m proud. And that's why I wanted
people to understand that sometimes we don't see  those who are inspiring us, and they're right in
front of us. They're right there. Uh, Verity had  her dad, you know, uh, Nitay-Yair had his mom.
These are people that we don't see what they're  actually doing for us, and then all of a sudden
it [Snaps] clicks. That they're important to us.  So, this is what I wanted people to understand,
how valuable those people are around us. And-and  I have so many people to thank along the way.
-Indeed, those families mean so much to us and  teach us so much about life. Here's a question
that I’d love for all three of you to answer. How  did you modify your speech for a: your virtual
audience, and b: for your international  audience? And we'll go to Verity first.
-Thank you, thank you, Margaret. A lot of my  modifications happened from practicing with
clubs around the world and it was so helpful  for me because there was things in my speech,
like we lived in what we call a caravan, but when  I practiced in the United States they were like,
“We would call it a campervan,” and then I could  just tweak and change words slightly which was
so helpful. And in terms of the virtual  space, I think where we're lucky is we've
had a year-and-a-half of getting used to doing  this virtually. I was so inspired watching last
year's contest and particularly Mike Carr's  winning speech and how he used the screen. So,
you know, he and his fellow contestants paved the  way for me to play in this format. So, that for me
wasn't the difficult part. What was-was exciting  for me was getting the feedback from audiences
in Bangladesh, in India, Australia, UK, America,  and just finding language and imagery that had
as broad a universal connection. Otherwise,  if I’m only getting feedback in South Africa,
we often don't realize that we're just coming from  one point of view. Without this virtual world I
don't know if I would have been able to make it  as accessible as I feel like I did in the end.
-It was a real advantage this year wasn't it? And  yes, you are truly all pioneers here. Nitay-Yair,
how did you modify your speech for a: your virtual  audience and b: your international audience?
-This is a very, very interesting question,  Margaret, and I’ll answer it in two levels:
I think…for me this is about creating art. It's  called the art of public speaking, not public
speaking. And when you look at it as art you  need to go outside of the box and-and-and go as
crazy as you can, and then turn it down based on  feedback. And I had great, uh, coaches this year,
Pres Vasilev coached me this year and I thank you  very much. And Lou Beaton, who's listening I hope,
thank you as well. And the reason I  mentioned that is because you take these
crazy ideas and then they help you tone it  down to what's maybe palatable to the audience,
as opposed to scare the audience. Some of the  stuff I wanted to do perhaps were too extreme
for the virtual, uh, sense, but the feedback that  you get is great. So, that's number one you need,
that circle of confidence, uh, and obviously  Bill and-and Sherry helped on that too. The
other thing is the clubs visits and-and the  greatest advantage—I’m a fairly new toastmaster,
I’m only two years and a big toastmaster and this  year people like Keith Hardy and Janet open and
Alicia as well open the door for me, because I  don't know how many clubs, to visit over I don't
know 70 clubs around the world. And when you test  the messages, especially in my semi-final speech,
in-in Africa, or in Vietnam, or in Singapore,  or in the United States and I think Verity
touched on a very important point: your message  needs to be global. It needs to be simple and
global. You can't use terms that people won't  understand in different countries, and I have
originally at the beginning, so the feedback is  extremely important. A simple message, but the
key to me is to focus on your message and deliver  it in an artful way. If I can summarize it I just
focus on the art. But support your message, yeah. -I love-I love that phrasing that public speaking
is an art, and that is truly, absolutely  correct. Roger, it's your turn now.
How did you modify your speech for your virtual  audience and for your international audience?
-Well for my final speech I had  created that speech a few years ago
and when I was, again as many of you have said  already, I worked with Pres Vasilev as well
in the first part of it in trying to create it  and-and have it for the in-person audience. And
I remember once we realized of course now that  we were going to be doing it online, there's a
lot of things that you have to change. I mean some  of the things that you would have in your speech,
and I’m sure that, uh, many of my other fellow  contestants can say the same thing, is that you
may have a moment where you're connecting with an  audience and you're looking one-on-one with them,
well now you're only looking at this little screen  right here, and you're trying so hard to make sure
that you can still bring your message through, and  they would feel it on the other side of that lens.
And that was what we had-I had to change when  I came to-when it came to the speech. So,
I worked with Craig Valentine this year and  he was instrumental in helping me to develop
the funny parts, the emotional parts, how to bring  it so that it can connect. But most importantly,
two people that I must-must thank and that  is Catherine McKenzie, who is the greatest
coach ever, and also Neil Dunsmore, who is a  great friend of mine, and we worked tirelessly
to make sure that we were able to work through  this little screen here and make it work. And
with regards to the global side of it, I will  say this: our stories are a gateway to our souls,
and it's the pathway to the audience's heart.  And what we try to do is make sure that when,
at least for myself, whatever message that I’m  sending out there, it is going to be universal.
You know, our stories are personal, but our  message has to be universal. And that was the
key to do something that, yes, could be personal  in my story, but the message itself everybody can
take away from, and that was important to me. -We did definitely feel all your-all eight
speeches, they were just so remarkable.  And definitely, you countered our souls
with that-that, uh, entry point there. So, I  have another question for all three of you.
How has Toastmasters helped you personally and  professionally? But this time we will start with
Nitay-Yair. Would you like to  answer the first time-for the first-
-Oh, God. This is-I’m going to embarrass  myself now, but heck with it, let's do it. So,
when I got married to my wife, Simone, who I my-my  nickname for her is “Bundle of love with big brown
eyes,” that's what the name big brown eyes come  from, that's my nickname for her, and that's why I
named all the other characters based on the eyes.  And we got married and she's not a toastmaster,
I wasn't a toastmaster at the time, and she did  this speech in our wedding, and she killed it.
She would have beat everyone today on the  speech. I’m biased by the way, sorry, Verity.
So, the-the-the-and then I did my speech, and  it was a disaster. It was an absolutely bomb
in my own wedding and I thought, “Okay, that  needs to change. That is that is not good.”
Uh, and I was very—believed or not, very shy.  I’m still very shy, and-and I don't necessarily
feel comfortable speaking in front of a large  audience, so the Toastmaster-Toastmasters journey,
I joined this club in the City Tattersalls  club—which I represent today—and it took me
six months to do my icebreaker. I was that afraid.  Six months to do my icebreaker. But once I did my
icebreaker, uh, my mentor Mike Keanu MacCallum and  Peter Anderson as well immediately came and said,
uh, “You need to do the International Speech  Contest.” …on the same year! And-and what it did,
it-it-what Toastmaster's environment or the  mentors that I have in Toastmasters did, they gave
me confidence. And the thing is you have a skill  set but until you have the confidence to use the
skill set, it's just a skill set that is buried  somewhere underneath the ground. So, what it did,
it elevated the confidence. But beyond that, it  created a network of supporters and people who
help you push toward your dream going forward.  And that is something that you-just doesn't exist
anywhere else. People you don't even-there's  some people who help me who I haven't even met
physically. Who I haven't even met, and  they live in the US, I live in Australia,
and-and I just-it's incredible. So, how did it  help me? Confidence. Absolutely confidence. You
know, we all have something burning inside,  the question is how do you bring it out?
For me that was Toastmasters. -That was a beautiful story beautiful,
beautiful story and I hope we will hear the  speech about you and your wife, uh, a full
five-to-seven minutes and not-on another time but  thank you for that. And the Toastmaster family
is definitely remarkable we'll-we are a unique  organization; only things like that happen here.
Roger, your turn. How has Toastmasters  helped you personally and professionally?
-Well, I’ll share my story. When I took over the  family business I used to walk into a lot of the
companies that we work with and they knew me while  my dad was around as just ‘hey it's Roger, how you
doing, Roger? What's going on?’ And when I took  over the business, you saw the change in how they
reacted to me and it was more like, ‘oh, here's  the owner so let's, uh, let's see what he's
about.’ And I remember sitting in an executive  office one day and he had just become the new
supervisor of the company that we work with,  and it was the first time ever I encountered
trying to speak to an introvert, and I had  no idea how to have a conversation with him,
and I remember leaving his office and coming  back to mind and saying some words that I
can't say because we're Toastmasters. I  couldn't say it and of course I looked up
how to improve my speaking abilities,  and that's how I got into Toastmasters.
And I’ll never forget my first speech that I did  when I did my icebreaker. There was a gentleman
there named Sanjay Sharma and once I finished  he came over he tapped my shoulders, and I think
everybody has one of these stories…I’m hoping.  But he tapped my shoulder after, and he goes,
“You're gonna be a champion one day, I can  feel it. I know it, I know it in my soul,”
and I laughed at him. Well, I’m not laughing  anymore, thank you, Sanjay, for that. So, that's
where it is for me. Personally and professionally,  Toastmasters has helped me build my confidence and
be able to feel comfortable speaking, whether  in person or right now on the virtual stage.
-Thank you for sharing that story too, very  special and precious—I guarantee no one said
that to me, “you will be champion,” so, they only  say it to those that are-have it within them. Well
done, Roger. Verity, how has Toastmasters  helped you personally and professionally?
-I joined Toastmasters for fun 10 years ago.  My sister had joined it to overcome her fear
of public speaking and I used to go to meetings  just to support at Two Oceans Toastmasters and I
loved it. I would do table topics and I thought it  was great. I was a professional singer and already
speaking at the time, so it was really like  this is something interesting for me to do once
a month. But I was also moments away from living  in the spare room and suffering from quite severe
depression and anxiety. And so, how Toastmasters  helped me was personally, it put me into an
organization where suddenly I had a purpose bigger  than myself. I was invited to join the committee
and I joined as a treasurer and someone who did  very bad at maths, I couldn't believe they were
trusting me with the books. But suddenly I was  part of a team, and I actually joined a second
club so that I would have a reason to get up on  a Wednesday morning and go to a meeting. I was
really suffering from bad depression at the time.  And it was a conscious choice, this organization
is going to help me. There's people here, there's  community, there's a sense of camaraderie. And so,
I kept showing up…and I had to overcome my  arrogance that I was already sorted as a speaker,
because my sister, Kay, in the club contest in  2012 beat me and I was very unimpressed because
she'd only done a cc6 and she went on to come  second to Ryan Avery in the semi-finals that year.
And I suddenly learned that you need to read  the manual and there is always something you
could learn, and you have to be mentored, and  you can't think you know everything. And so,
I’m only here today because I’ve spent nine years  listening in this organization, taking feedback
and leaning into the leadership opportunities it's  given me, because that's where it's really changed
me. It's changed the way I run my business, after  being treasurer, I’ve never struggled to get money
out of a client again. It's been amazing, so it's  been life-changing and I might gloss over the fact
that I was in a spare room eating ice cream and  Netflix, but it was a very dark time in my life,
and this organization gave me purpose  through that. So, I will be forever grateful
and forever looking for ways to  give back to this organization.
-We're so thankful that you got over the ice  cream and the, uh, Netflix binging for sure.
And thank you for that about reading the manual,  now the project, right? You-you have to read-yes,
do the work. Do the work together. Thank you  all for those answers, they were beautiful.
But right now, we want to hear from Verity on how  many times have you presented that speech you gave
during the World Championship of Public Speaking,  and what did your coaches or mentors say or do
that made the difference in your decision  to pursue this World Champion title?
-So, the speech I gave today I wrote exactly 100  days ago. And the reason I know that is it came to
me at two in the morning and the original version,  although very similar to the story I told today,
was also sharing that I had done one of the things  I did based on my father's advice was a 100 happy
days challenge—to just take pictures of things  that made me happy. And so, when I wrote the
speech I thought, “you know what?” And I looked  at the date, and I was like, “Gosh, it's exactly a
hundred days till the world finals and if this was  the speech I would give, I’m gonna do my hundred
happy days while I give the speech.” And really,  today has been the happiest day of my life.
But I’ve given the speech hundreds of times.  It's changed its message multiple times
and through working with Lawrence Miller as my-my  coach and he just gently pushed me and guided me,
he didn't ever kind of push me into directions I  didn't want to go in, but he held the space for me
to question decisions I was making, try different  things. And through the feedback I had, we only
ended up—I’d write a different story two weeks ago  and I actually would like to—so, the same the same
speech, just the thread came through and that was  feedback, uh, from a toastmaster in South Africa,
and he just he made one comment in his evaluation  to me, and it made me re-look at the whole speech.
And suddenly it just came together. So, I will be  forever grateful. And that is why I say to anyone
if you choose to go on this journey, deliver your  speech to as many people as you can. Suck it up,
take the feedback, it's not always easy; my ego  has been bruised and some of it's been brutal, but
I’ve had to listen. And go, “Is there something,  and if three people have said the same thing,
am I open to change?” So, I have been giving  this speech for 100 days, it has changed me,
it has shaped me, it has challenged me. But I  would never -would never do it any other way
other than rewriting and rewriting and  redelivering and tweaking and changing,
up until the day of the finals there was little  moments that were still coming to me. So,
I’m sure there's 10 other versions I could give  but I’m very grateful that I’ve now done it.
-Well, that was outstanding to hear how many  times it takes, and really, how long you have
to work at something till that ultimate idea,  that concept, that really getting it within you,
how long that can sometimes take. So, for all of  us, we need to keep working, keep working. We have
so many questions from the audience. We're going  to go to audience questions now. So, the first one
is, “There is a thin line between being  vulnerable and over sharing. How do each of you
navigate this fine line?” So, let's  go to Roger first and then Nitay-Yair.
-That is an absolutely great question. The reality  is-is as speakers the way you connect with your
audience is being vulnerable. Is allowing them  to see that inner human side of you. I think it's
very important to share that. Now the thin line,  yes, you don't want to share too much sometimes
because you don't want to expose yourself, but I  kind of look at it from a different perspective.
And that is that there is somebody in that  audience whether we are in person or virtually,
there's somebody there that is waiting to hear  a particular message. And sometimes when we as
speakers go out there and we speak, it could take  just you opening up yourself and talking about
something that has happened to you that will help  that one person in the audience. And I’ll give you
a quick example. I went and I spoke once at  an open house and I talked about, you know,
fear in an event that had happened to me before  and this gentleman came up to me after the event
and he said, “You know what, it's funny you  did that. I wasn't going to come here today,
but somebody said, ‘you know, come and see  this guy.’” And when I finished, he said,
“I was going to go to my lawyers at-after work  at about four o'clock today and sign papers
to divorce my wife because I thought she was  the one that was at fault for everything that
happened in our relationship.” He said, “After  I heard your speech, I realized it was me that
needed to change the things that were going on  with me. And now we're trying to reconcile that
we're going to go and reconcile things.” These are  those moments that you as a speaker just go, “Oh,
I didn't know I could do that,” but that's  why being vulnerable and allowing yourself
to share your stories—It can help someone else  to cure their own problems that they're having.
-Absolutely. What a gift this tool is, right, to  be able to share with others and have impact on
their life and influence them in a positive way.  Thank you for doing that. So, Nitay-Yair, over to
you. I’ll read the question again to you from the  audience. “There's a thin line between building
vulnerable-” sorry, “-to being vulnerable and over  sharing. How did you navigate this fine line?”
-The truth is I’m not sure I’m able to navigate  that fine line and that's-that's the absolute
truth. Um, my personal view is this: if there's  something, a message that is burning in you, you
need to get it out. And you need to-to put all the  shields and all the walls that you put around you
and just share it. And it makes me emotional  now because that's just the truth. And if you
share your message raw, people will  connect. But you need to be careful;
you need to lift them up at the end  of it. You need to open your heart,
say, “This is who I am. You may not like it,  but this is who I am,” and then close it and
take them back up because you-you don't want them  more depressed than-than when they come and saw
your speech. But unless-unless you go in and show  them the real you, um, I don't-I don't believe
that there will be any connection. That's my  personal view. I’m not probably the best person
to answer that question because I-I don't know  how to separate it too, I really don't. Yeah.
-Thank you, yeah, thank you for that share,  you—and all of you really did lift us up,
you were marvelous at that. All right,  Verity, I’ll-I’ll read it again. “There's
a thin line between being vulnerable and over  sharing; how did you navigate this fine line?”
-Well similar to Nitay-Yair, I’m-I am a very  honest person; my name means truth, so I tend
to speak about what I’ve dealt with. But I think  the-the line for me is and-and I can't remember
where I heard this, but they say you should never  speak about something until you can laugh about
it. So, even if it was a heartbreaking,  you know, shameful, difficult situation,
don't speak about it until you've dealt with it.  So, I tend to talk about quite difficult things
that I’ve gone through, and I-I can laugh at  myself and I’m not afraid to share my flaws. I’m
less than perfect and-and I talk about  that often, but I’m not using my talk as
personal therapy. And maybe that is  where we see something as over sharing,
is we're using the talk to maybe try  and process it in front of an audience,
whereas the audience as Nitay-Yair said wants  to be lifted up. So, be honest. Be vulnerable.
Open up your arms, you know, own your shame.  People grow and-and Roger said this as well,
